Fewer than two in a hundred new cars in America have a clutch pedal.
From a stop, the engine doesn't touch them.
It spins a fan in a can of oil, and the oil spins a second fan.
That's why you can stop without stalling.
Then comes the real trick: one set of gears.
Hold the outer ring, and the output crawls. Low gear.
Lock it all together: one to one.
Hold the carrier, and it turns backwards. Reverse.
Clutches do the holding, squeezed by oil and switched by a computer.
Ford and GM's ten-speed stacks four of these sets.
